utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Thank you, Mr. President. We'll get going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll -- thank you very much. We'll get going and finish up shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we were on Exhibit 507, a Zvornik Brigade workbook. If we could go to page 31 of that workbook. And if you could remind us that -- what date that is -- should be.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular date is 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are you pointing out here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, I'm pointing out a notation at 1750 hours between the Zvornik SUP, calling the duty officer and asking for Lieutenant Colonel Popovic to call them. I only point this out insomuch as I don't have any additional information that would go around, however it just reflects the continued presence of Lieutenant Colonel Popovic in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be page 32 of the English language translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last bullet that I've highlighted. In this particular instance noting that message from Zlatar that a parcel set off from Badem half an hour ago. And that it was reported to the IKM at 2015 hours. This is a group of reinforcements that are finally setting off from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on 16 July and will arrive within the hour. If you can move up three bullets, there's a notation that says men from Bratunac are in Orahovac. Those individuals are members of the two platoons of the Bratunac Brigade who arrived on the 15th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, what's the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is -- should be 507, the English translation of the workbook, and then we went to the particular pages on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 33 of the English language translation, I just highlighted the passage, the second bullet, that 30 soldiers arrived at 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tie that into any of the material we saw last week in particular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular one and the references of the reinforcements tie into the intercept on 16 July 1995, between Popovic and Rasic, and then later where Colonel Cerovic is brought up to speed on the reinforcements that have been arriving in the Bratunac Brigade zone during the late afternoon/early evening hours of 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just -- we note at the bottom of page 33, there is, again, a mention of rifle grenades and hand grenades to be sent to Orahovac. And then back of page 32 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reference --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Bratunac Brigade men in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you relate that in any way to what we have seen regarding prisoners and executions at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't. In this particular instance, my understanding of the general combat situation is that on the evening of 15 July, the unit that had come in from Bratunac on 15 July was deployed. And as a result of the combat activities had been cut off and had been forced to essentially retreat through the woods was lost for a good portion of the night and did not show up again on a major roadway until approximately noon on 16 July 1995. So I attribute this provisioning of getting weapons and grenades and ammunition to that unit as an attempt to resupply that unit after a night in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to the next reference that you've highlighted.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 34 of the English language translation, at the second bullet, I've highlighted a reference where at 2210 hours, the first infantry battalion asked for one loader, one dump truck with a tarp to be in Pilica at 0800 hours. That would be 17 July 1995. And the comment that this is being conveyed to Jokic and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, what do you think that first sentence involves, talking about the loader and excavator and dump truck to Pilica at 0800 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we understand the context of executions at Branjevo Military Farm and at the Pilica Dom on 16 July, while the executions occurred, the actual activity to begin to bury the bodies at Branjevo Military Farm as well as vehicles to pull the bodies out of the Pilica Dom and then bring them to where they would also be buried, did not begin until the next day, the 17th. So in that respect, I believe this indicates that the 1st Battalion is calling to ensure that the equipment they will need to begin this operation is available the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 1st Battalion, why would it be the 1st Battalion, aside from that it says it here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Branjevo Military Farm and the Dom of culture in Pilica are both in the 1st Battalion area of operations or in their zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then it says, the next sentence, convey to Jokic and Milosevic. Who do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given what they're asking for, I believe the reference is that this particular case Jokic is Major Dragan Jokic, the chief of engineering, and Milosevic is Captain First Class Sretan Milosevic who is the assistant for rear services. Within the context of what they are asking for, those are the two likely individuals they would be coordinating with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other references in this book that you want to...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 35 of the English language translation, just a reference that members of the reserve or Worker's Battalion are now joining the men from Bratunac. They're given one set of ammunition and they're being taken up to a specific part of the line and that that line is to be taken up at 0800 hours on 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's next?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final reference that I have in this book is now on the morning of the 17th of July 1995, and it will be page 36 of the English language translation. Roughly sometime after 5.40 in the morning on the 17th, the 1st Battalion again apparently is called, asking if the engineering machines have been secured. It's reported the situation is normal in their zone, and there's a phrase, Trbic to report. In this particular context, Trbic, not only is he a security officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, but I also believe that during this period from the -- to the day of the 16th, in the evening of the 16th, 17th, and the morning of the 17th, Captain Milorad Trbic is also performing as the Zvornik Brigade duty officer that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, yes, any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think I have a little bit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. A little bit that will last five days?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I just need a second, Your Honour, to get this. Sorry. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On direct examination, you were asked on Friday, that was November 14th, 2003, whether during the Krstic -- your testimony in Krstic, whether you had made a mistake with respect to Mr. Erdemovic's information. Do you recall that question being posed to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, just to be precise for the record and for our analysis of this mistake, if we could just put on the ELMO the relevant portion of that exchange between you and Mr. McCloskey. I have a copy. It's on page 73, and I'm using the -- 74. Now, if we could just go down the line starting with number 1 on page 73, it starts at the bottom of the page, you'll see the question being posed to you and the question is. "Q. In your Krstic testimony, did you make a mistake in relating Mr. Erdemovic's information?" And your answer was, and I'm going to read the whole answer, it will take us into the next page. "A. I did. And I recognised when I reviewed my transcript testimony approximately a week ago on that. And I had misspoke, and one of the things I asked for was as soon as I recognised that I had said that, the tape be checked, because attributed to me is the observation that Erdemovic had said" - it says here 'sent' - "said men from the Bratunac Brigade. And I would like to go on record that at the very beginning of my association with this case, I have always known that Mr. Erdemovic has always said that" - we're into the next page we're into the next page if you wanted to follow along - "that it was men or soldiers from Bratunac. He had never indicated that they were men from the Bratunac Brigade, and that is a fact that I know. And that is why I asked for clarification as to whether that was actually something I had said. If I did say it," and I underscore the if part. "If I did say, I did misspeak." Now, for the sake of clarity of the record, I like to visit the actual exchange with respect to that matter during the Krstic case. And so, again, if I could have the assistance of Madam Usher, we'll put it on the ELMO. And this can be found on the transcript page 4.915. I'm going to be reading line 7 to 17, testimony taken 29 June 2000. If we could look at that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, that's the wrong extract.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. Okay. If I could have a moment. I believe it is the right one. If we could look at -- I'm going to start with the question which starts with line 7 on this page. And if you could just follow along. And -- now, you posed the question. "Q. Now, as the conversation ends with General Krstic says, I'll see what I can do, this is around a 10.00 a.m. July 15th conversation, with the 10th Divisionary Unit, get any assistance from the Drina Corps assets on July 16th in the executions at the Branjevo Farm? "A. What we see in the time sequence is on the morning of the 16th, first, the 10th Divisionary is at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. It then goes to the Branjevo military farm. And according to the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic, while they are in the commission of the actual execution, members of the Bratunac Brigade show up at the execution site and assist them for that phase of the execution, or, in effect, continue the execution." Now, having looked at this portion, I guess we can take off the if you said it part of your answer on Friday, and replace it with that you did, in fact, say it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, you may choose to do that, but I will go back and review the tapes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But for the sake of argument, I will concede that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, help me out here, help me out here because you just piqued my interest. On Friday you said that this was alarming to you when you saw it a week prior to your testimony and that you asked to look at the tapes, because how could you possibly make such a mistake. I assume - I assume - before coming in here and confessing error, as you did, albeit in a qualifying fashion on Friday, you must have taken the time to listen to the tapes. Question: Did you listen to the tapes? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, those tapes are sitting in my house in Atlanta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There is such a thing as Federal Express, though, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is a question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is something as Federal Express, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- I notice here, assuming that the tape is correct, I see you've chosen two particular phrases which are somewhat significant. One, "according to the testimony." Correct? It says it right there. And then you say "members of the Bratunac Brigade," right? You see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, follow along with me and I will now demonstrate to you what we know in my business as the concept of looping, where you take a portion of the question -- answer, and then make it part of the next question, thereby, highlighting its importance. The following question. "Q. And there are intercepts that support the presence of the Bratunac Brigade at that site also, is that correct, that we'll get to later?" Let me read it again. "Q. And there are intercepts that support the presence of the Bratunac Brigade" -- you see, that's the looping part, the highlighting part "at the site that we'll get to later?" Now here, one would think, one, the questioner he would -- either he knew or would have been aware that you had misspoken and received no correction but indeed we see an incorporation of your previous answer into the question. Now, let's look at the answer to see whether you correct yourself at that point. Assuming, of course, you said all these things which you will be able to verify at some point. "A. There are intercepts which support the Bratunac Brigade at that site, and there are written orders which support the presence of Bratunac Brigade units in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade during the period as well." My to you, sir, is: Do you recall making this statement to that question posed to you by the examiner on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall making -- do you recall that answer, giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so if you recall the answer, would it be fair to say that -- if you recall this particular answer, that in all likelihood, you also recall the question that was previously posed? That is the one where you mention "members of the Bratunac Brigade," a fact which you knew at the time, as you have confessed on Friday, to have been false.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I mean, clearly I can see what I have said up on the ELMO. I recognised with respect to the comment about the Bratunac Brigade, but as soon as I came across it again in my own review of my transcripts that it was incorrect, and I brought it immediately to Mr. McCloskey's attention. So, I mean in that respect, yes, I recognise that it was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But my question is this, sir: We've seen an admirable demonstration over the past week of a command of facts like I've never seen before, and yet, on a very important issue, an issue that has found itself even in the UN report, which we'll get to, an issue that the office of the Prosecution, for whom you worked for had been trying to get Drazen Erdemovic to please say Bratunac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The point has been made. That's an absolute misstatement of the situation. He's accusing the Prosecution of all kinds of ill-doings, he's accusing Mr. Butler. The point is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's also speculation, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm demonstrating a point, Your Honour. Because I'm using the same analytical techniques that the gentleman used in formulating his own analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you make a point, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll visit another point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, do you know whether Mr. Erdemovic testified before you on this occasion or after you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular case, I believe he testified before me, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would that you would have closely followed that testimony and in all likelihood would have read the transcript prior to taking the stand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for a fact that I did so, but that would be a fair assumption, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you hadn't, in all likelihood, you would have been briefed by the lawyer or lawyers that were involved in the preparation of and the direct examination of Mr. Erdemovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by the phrase "brief," but again I was familiar with the testimony and the witness statements of Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, just for clarity sake, because it's an issue that I think is relevant to this case, I'd like to visit the Erdemovic testimony, the relevant portion, with respect to this issue. So if we could have the assistance of Madam Usher, I would like to show you -- I would like to put on the ELMO from the Krstic trial, page 3.132, and if we could look at lines 18 to 25. You will see that the question begins at 11, line 11, and then on line 16, page 3.132, this was 22 May, 2000, which indeed was -- preceded your testimony this time. The examiner is none other than Mr. Harmon. It says, the answer that Mr. Erdemovic gives that: "All the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment did not participate in these executions. About -- between 1.00 and 2.00, members came from Bratunac, so that I heard when somebody said that people from Bratunac had come to assist. And they took over the killing of those people, in the same way as our group had done, only they recognised some of those people and they took it out on them. I think that one of the men from Bratunac was a native of Srebrenica and he recognised some." If we go on to the next page, he says, and again I apologise. We'll get it right this morning. Sorry. He says: "I remember he recognised the butcher from Srebrenica, and I know that he said, you're a good man, but I have to kill you. I know that you were not a nationalist." So here, clearly, would you not agree with me, he says he's asked a question, a particular question, a specific question, and he says that they were from Bratunac, no mention of the brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, further down that same page it says -- there's a question on line 20. "I'd like to explore now the identities of these people who came from Bratunac. First of all, Mr. Erdemovic, how were they dressed?" "A. They were, as far as I can remember, all dressed in uniforms of the Army of Republika Srpska. Only one was wearing a uniform that I could see," and the next page which is 3.314 And, here, if you could have it handy with you, all of this. I truly apologise. Mr. Butler, if we could have your assistance. I notice you're pretty handy with the ELMO there. So you can just... Thank you. So as I was saying. He says: "As far -- I recognise him as being the uniform of the American army. That's on line 1, 3.134 Who was it who said the men from Bratunac had arrived?" Then there was an answer. "I think it was Brano, but I'm not certain. I think possibly it was him, because I saw him first, shake hands with them." And then there's an exchange. So clearly at least at this point in Erdemovic's testimony, we begin to identify one individual. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we learn that, one, he seemed to be from Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he was wearing an American uniform, which is slightly distinctive, in light of what everybody else was wearing in the VRS at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, at some point later on, and if we could go to pages 3.135, you will recall, because I'm sure you were involved in the preparation of all of this, there were some exhibits that were shown to -- that were shown to Mr. Erdemovic. In fact, there were exhibits 173, 174, and 175. Now, I'm going to hand you these exhibits. And I have -- and we need to go into closed session, Your Honour, for the questions that I'm going to be posing -- private session, so we don't have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have copies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we won't put the photos on the ELMO. And once we are in private, we can openly discuss this at our leisure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we've covered that ground, I want to go back to that issue where we started off with respect to the mistake you made during the Krstic trial, because I note on another occasion when you testified, once again we seem to have a slight mishap or misstep or however you wish to put it. So if we could turn to the second time that you testified. And if I could direct your attention to the Krstic trial transcript. It's Monday 17 July 2000 and if I could have the assistance of Madam Usher. Thank you. Now, if we could look at pages 5.149 and if we go through lines 1 -- 3 to 11. So part of the -- 3 is part of the question that is being posed to you. We don't need to read the entire question, so we'll start at line 3, page 5.149, 17 July 2000. "So in any event, Vujadin Popovic says in about six different ways that Vidoje Blagojevic's people were late. How does this tie in with the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic?" And I take it from here we can glean that we're talking about what I call the "up there" intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the one the Popovic and Rasic, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're with me. We're on the same wavelength now. All right. Now. The answer that you give is. "A. As Drazen Erdemovic describes the execution process which occurred at the Branjevo Military Farm on 16 July, he recounts that initially the members of the 10th Sabotage Unit were conducting the executions. He also further notes that at a point in time soldiers whom he believes to be members of the Bratunac Brigade arrive at the Branjevo Military Farm and, in effect, take over the execution process." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This was the specific notation that I came across when preparing for my own testimony here that I tagged as something that I recognised as incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So just as I have perhaps -- well, not perhaps, just has I had been unable to find in your rebuttal one correction that you made, it seems that you were unable to find the earlier mishap that you stated with respect to how you were tying in the members of the Bratunac Brigade through the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look to the next question, again just for instructive purposes using -- because at some point we're going to try to analyse this and put it all together. We don't see a correction from the questioner, in other words asking you as he had done last week on two or three occasions, no more than that, perhaps you had misspoken, perhaps you meant men from Bratunac. There's no attempt to jingle your memory and correct you, is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the inference that the Prosecution is somehow --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is no inference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to listen to Mr. McCloskey's statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler concluded in his testimony last time that the Bratunac Brigade was what Mr. Erdemovic was talking about. That was based on an intercept. And that is what led to this mistake, and it's coming completely out of context from Mr. Karnavas. There is now new information on this point that was completely cleared up by Mr. Butler, and these inferences that there's -- that he's trying to make are just -- are not appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question is that whether this witness who has already corrected his mistake he made during the previous statement, there is no need to attack the other side, unless you have a lot of evidence to say that the Prosecution tried to hide this information. But up to now, we believe that during the direct examination by the Prosecution, they take the initiative to ask some questions, they give the witness the opportunity to correct their mistake. So concentrate your cross-examination on the issue which is directly related to your client, rather than attacking the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, for the record -- if I may for the record, first and foremost, nobody is attacking the Prosecution. They may be slightly embarrassed, nobody is attacking them, no inferences are being drawn. Secondly, at some point in time, you will be asked to evaluate the gentleman's testimony and his reports. There are times that we will show throughout the process of cross-examination where the gentleman states one particular analysis, and we believe that there might be another one. This is a method by which I'm trying to demonstrate, using their own analytical techniques how one could get the same reaction that I just got from Mr. McCloskey, that somehow we're inferring that they're hiding. We're not inferring that. Secondly, I'm pointing out that they had an opportunity to clear up the record. They knew. The questioners knew. Harmon who knew. McCloskey knew. They didn't make that. Now I'm not suggesting it was purposeful. But in all likelihood, it was an innocent mishap. They're thinking about the next question. However, if we have a devious mind, we may think they're doing something devious. What I'm trying to demonstrate is there are two sides to the coin. I'm not suggesting they did anything wrong in this case. I know they are both honourable men. That's not my point. I'm driving another point and I'm trying to show that there may be some flaws in the analytical process in this case, that's all. Because at the end of the day I think there are some issues with certain pieces of evidence where they're open or subject to a variety of interpretations. We don't have enough of the information and I think Mr. Butler would agree with me that there are no absolute truths in this particular case with most of the evidence because a lot of it deals with circumstantial evidence. So that's my point. And I'll move on. I think I've made my point on that. I think I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on. We are professional Judges, we could understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but I would feel more comfortable if I have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point -- now, you did indicate that, I believe, on Friday, if we go back to that little exchange, that you corrected yourself on rebuttal. We'll discuss that at some point when I'm able to see that portion of your testimony, however, I do want to cover another aspect of the rebuttal that was brought out through the questioning process, particularly by the Judges in that case. So if I could have the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court. I'm switching a little bit in light of the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me -- let's look at at least a portion of the rebuttal of your testimony from the Krstic trial, and if you could just look through it first to see whether you recognise that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand it, you testified more than one time on rebuttal. Is that correct? I think it was twice.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on this particular -- this time it was on 23 March 2001 that you testified. Now, if we could direct your attention -- well, first, before I direct your attention, during that rebuttal process, there was some discussion with respect to one particular piece of evidence which was a tape of the kill 'em all portion of an intercept. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that's a bit of an understatement, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that was a major issue, was it not, during the trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that it was a major legal and evidentiary issue with respect to the Prosecution's case. From my perspective, it had very little analytical relevance for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get to that. But here is one of the -- this is what we might call, even in your parlance, a smoking gun. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I testified with respect to Srebrenica, I thought it was something of the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your opinion today as you sit here that that tape had no evidentiary value?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe I said that while I understood that it could be used as an inferential piece with respect to determining or not determining genocidal effect, that I didn't believe it had any value with respect to the events pertaining to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, before we get to that part of the mental process that went in and whether to include it or not include it and the strategy that went behind it, you were asked a question, I believe it was the President of the Court, Judge Rodrigues, who had indicated to you that the tape was a montage, and that could be found on page 9.086, question starts with lines 6 to line 9. He asked you that it was -- whether --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Krstic said it's 100 per cent montage. And then there is this lengthy answer or complete as we should say. Then it ends up with on the very next page, page 9087 on page 14 -- line 14 you say: "And in this case, given the balance of probabilities and given everything I know about it, I'm fairly certain this is not a montage." Do you recall making that statement to the question posed to you by the President of the Trial Chamber during the Krstic on 23 March 2001?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words from your answer, can I conclude that it is your professional opinion and the opinion of the members of the Prosecution, a team of which you were and remain a member of, that that tape was authentic, reliable, and relevant -- or is it the relevant part that you have problems with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking in context that the question with respect to Judge Rodrigues was on the issue of the deception or whether the tape was fabricated, it is -- it was then and it remains now my opinion that it is, in fact, authentic. So that's the first part of your question. Reliable insomuch as it is an accurate transcription of the context of the conversation, yes, I believe it is. Relevant, I again -- I have always made it clear that with respect to the events surrounding Srebrenica that I don't particularly believe it is relevant, given the fact that the crime scenes for Srebrenica, which kind of mandate the context of my report, close out at approximately 19 or 20 July 1995, with the exception of the reburial. So given that this conversation occurs on 02 August of 1995 and directly with respect to Zepa, which is not under investigation, I don't believe it's relevant. That's the light in which I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it didn't meet the relevancy test as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with respect to the crimes at Srebrenica, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this may be a good time, Your Honour, to break, because I'm going to launch into a segment of my cross that will take a half hour just on this issue of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I failed to notice this morning that David Kay from the United States, I'm sure you saw it, was here for the initial part of Mr. Butler's cross. Mr. Karnavas and I have had a chance to speak and we do not anticipate any U.S. Issues coming up on cross, so Mr. Kay has left and will come back probably for the cross of Mr. Jokic's cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for a small housekeeping matter, I made references from the Krstic case. So what was marked in Krstic as P173 should be marked for identification purposes as D77/1, what was then in Krstic as P174 should be in this case for identification D78/1. And what was marked in Krstic as P175 should be marked for identification as D79/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe we left off, Mr. Butler, where we were discussing this tape and the issue as it arose during the rebuttal of your testimony in Krstic. Now, for the sake of precision, if we could go to page 9.082 and I would like to read the pertinent scenes into the record and then from there we will begin to dissect it, if you will, and get into your analysis and mental process. You were asked a question by Judge Wald. My last question and answer again only if you're comfortable because I don't want to go outside any bounds, but you did say in your -- that when you first came across this or when you first analysed it, you said you didn't analyse it until late 1999, I think. And the next page starting with line 1, 9.083 page 9.083. "Now, I understand fully your explanation of why it is just didn't fall into place for your task of recording, from a military point of view, all the events which went on, but you did say yourself that you thought it would be powerful, and you knew there was a debate in the legal staff. I don't want to know anything about the backgrounds or people involved in that, but I guess my basic question, since you brought it up, was whether or not you participated in that debate with the legal staff or you're just saying you knew there was a debate in the legal staff?" And your answer is: "I was a party to those debates. I was a -- I was a major, significant party. I was fully integrated into the team and in the debates in the process, and --" and you're cut off by Judge Wald. Hence, he says: "So was the debate again, I don't want to know what the -- but did the debate concern whether to use that intercept in the case in-chief?" And your answer is, and by the way, when we're talking about the intercept, we're talking about the kill 'em all intercept. The actual video. Correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. The video that's derived from the intercept. It's actually an audiotape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The audiotape. I'm sorry, the audiotape. And so, the answer, your answer is: "The one aspect of the debate pertained to the fact that to use it in the case in-chief, if I felt that I needed it, meant that at the end of the day, the Defence would have a very long opportunity to come up with a well-rehearsed answer to what it was."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: "Well, I shouldn't ask you that. You're not a lawyer, but I was going to say, isn't that what the trial process is about? "A. Understanding that, but again from my perspective, when I look at the information -- I'm not naive as to the mechanicals involved, I mean, and I guess where -- fundamentally, to frame the argument, where that information falls is as a piece of military analysis, does that piece of information assist me in allowing the Court to understand General Krstic's role as a commander related to the crimes and everything else. "Now, having said that, I also understand that as a piece of information, it can be used as an indicator of the mental state of the accused, and I'm not qualified to pass on that." And Judge Wald, not giving up the point: "I'm not asking you. Just a last question. You said you analysed in late 1999. Did this, quote, debate take place around that time, or prior to trial, I guess is what I'm saying, to your knowledge? "A. The debate took place -- not only prior to but continuing during the case, the case in-chief. The final decision ultimately on where to use it wasn't until my narrative hit the final form, and from my point of view, I determined that I didn't need it." Now that we've got it into context, do you recall being posed those questions and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand your testimony earlier, you said that it was authentic, it was reliable, but it didn't meet your test of relativity. It wasn't relevant to your analysis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the association with the Srebrenica crime scenes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nonetheless you indicated that it was powerful, right, that was the term that you used. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, if it wasn't such a relevant piece of evidence, why pray tell, help me out here, why would there be such a debate inside the OTP, the Prosecution team, where you as a member, an integrated, an infiltrated member of this association, why would there be such a debate on whether to use it during the case in-chief or, as it turned out, a sabotaging technique on cross-examination once the accused was smoked out and put on the stand. Tell us. Explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I will at least take offense to the term infiltrated the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay. I took some liberties there, but you were integrated into it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply put, Mr. Karnavas, when I was doing my analysis of that as well as all the other intercepts in context, given that the focus of my report was strictly with respect to Srebrenica 1995 and that my analysis was that that particular conversation fell outside of that did not take away from the fact that it was viewed as a powerful piece of evidence, first and foremost with respect to confirming the actual authenticity of the intercepts themselves. Secondly, they're certainly, from a legal and more abstract perspective, perhaps, the phrase where General Krstic is telling them, Major Obrenovic, to kill them all, I suspect from the optics of the Court is very powerful. However, based on that conversation and as I also noted in my testimony, and I believe it was to Judge Wald with that respect, I was not prepared to conclude based on that comment in isolation that the intent behind that conversation was criminal in nature and I held open the possibility that it may very well had nothing to do with the commission of any crimes, given that we don't have any significant crimes with respect to Zepa to my knowledge. And it very much may have been a commander enthusiastically exhorting a subordinate commander to carry out his duty. So that is generally with respect to my perspective of those discussions that had carried on. Now, if you're going to ask my opinion on some of the more legal aspects of that, if you can frame those questions I would be happy to answer them. As it is often noted, I am not a lawyer. And while I am party to many of those debates, I don't get a vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to stick with this issue for a little bit, if you don't mind. I guess my -- I have to look at part of your answer and what troubles me a little bit is that you seem to imply, if I may use that word since it popped up earlier today, that us Defence lawyers are in the business of coaxing our clients on how to manipulate the evidence in our favour, in other words to put it bluntly and in the pedestrian form, we're in the business of assisting our clients in lying and coming up with excuses. That's how I read your language here, which is why you indicated you did not want to put that matter into your report and why it wasn't going to be used during the case in-chief. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that that would be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you not say that you didn't want the Defence to have a very long opportunity to come up with a well-rehearsed, your words, not mine, answer to what it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a misstatement of the evidence. The -- he never said that that was his intent and that's a misstatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour. Let me go back and read it. We have the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One aspect of the debate which you partook in pertained to the fact that "to use it in the case in-chief if I felt that I needed, if I felt that I needed it, meant that at the end of the day, the Defence would have a long opportunity to come up with a well-rehearsed answer to what it was." Now, at this point, sir, you were an integrated member, by your own words, of this Prosecution team, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would appear, at least from reading this, that you were not some independent operator, an independent analyst, but rather a strategist, a member of the strategic team of the office of the Prosecution in which you were going to analyse information and perhaps even put the spin required in order to get the case to where it needed to be to the satisfaction of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to your first question, yes, I am an integrated and strategic member of the Prosecution team with that respect. With respect to the second one, I think I worked very hard with respect to my analysis so that it has no spin. I suspect that if I'm remiss in that, you'll point that out. However, my goal as an analyst, certainly as it's been explained to me, and I think in a broader context with all the military analysts that have worked and do work for the Office of the Prosecutor, is that our goal is to try and place the material in as accurate a military context as possible. We trust that collectively as analysts by putting the information out in as accurate and correct a context as possible, that suits the overall needs of the Prosecutor in that respect. I don't know how to make that issue any more clear. I mean, obviously, sometimes it may not suit a specific Prosecutor or lawyer, but that is the general operating philosophy by which certainly the military and then the criminal analysts within the Office of the Prosecutor work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's dissect that a little bit. First of all, we know that this was a powerful piece of information that was reliable and authentic and that it was relative in the general period of time of the incidents surrounding Srebrenica. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was post-Srebrenica, and specifically had to do with issues well after what the Prosecution caps as the end of the Srebrenica crime scene period with respect to direct crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- but isn't it a fact that some Muslim men were out in the woods still trying to make their way to what was then known as the free territory. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so if they were remnants of the members of the Srebrenica municipality that were out there and if General Krstic did indeed -- was ordering one of his commanders in the Zvornik Brigade, which is right at the critical juncture where they're trying to pass into the free territory, and the General is saying, kill whoever you capture, would that not meet some indicia of relevance for this particular case? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in fact he used the phrase "kill whoever you capture," then the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did he use, what did he say, kill 'em all, right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the phrase is, and obviously why the controversy is aimed that way, it's kill them all and I believe he says later on, don't let any of them remain alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right and you're not a psychiatrist or a psychologist and neither you're a clairvoyant to know exactly what General Krstic meant at that time if indeed the tape is accurate. But needless to say, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to figure out that that is a vital piece of information that at least the trier of fact, that is the honourable members of this Tribunal should have before them in trying to reach as close as possible to the truth. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are we talking about the Krstic or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an issue of my report, and given the fact that I could not make any conclusion or even an assessment with respect to any potential criminality in nature, I didn't believe that it was relevant. And as I've always tried to note as part of my analysis, I try to make my analysis with that respect particularly in any issue where the Court might be invited to draw criminal intent, I try to make my analysis as conservative as possible in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what would the -- what could the harm have been. If you had, exercising your own independence, to have put it into your report with the caveat, with the qualification, that while we have this intercept, which purportedly is authentic and reliable, I do not think it has any relevance in this particular case. And then you go on to give the explanation that you so eloquently gave us just now. What would the harm have been to put that into the report so that at least the Defence lawyers and the Trial Chamber would have notice of this piece of information prior to and during the Prosecution case in-chief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer would be, if I were to chose to have taken that approach with this particular intercept, then how would I have justified not doing that with hundreds of other intercepts, which arguably would have fit that same criteria and may very well have nothing to do with the issues that I'm discussing. It is a -- so in that respect, I chose to be conservative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How many other intercepts, by the way, did you have where you had a live voice on that intercept that could be identified as a commander, a commander of a corps whom you thought and you believe to be at the apex of the criminal line with respect to this joint criminal enterprise? How many?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't of some lowly soldier or some captain first class or second class, but here we have a general of the Drina Corps. And you're telling us -- you're telling us as you sit here today that you didn't think that that was even worthy of a minor footnote in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, as I had indicated before the Krstic Trial Chamber in that respect, it again is a reflection of my trying to be as conservative in my analysis as possible. I think I put it quite bluntly, I'm not a charitable person with respect to this. If I thought that it had relevance with respect to commission of criminal acts and if I believed that I could tie it into that, I certainly would have used it. But I did not use it in that context because I could not make those issues of analysis -- I could not draw those conclusions, and I'm not prepared to invite the Court to entertain those inferences if I'm not prepared to be able to substantiate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are making inferences in this case, are you not, based on circumstantial evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And each one that I make I'm fully prepared to substantiate before the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, we'll going to get to that as well. But, I guess I'm still a little troubled. You say it's not relevant, it wasn't worthy to be in your report, yet there was this heated debate, a heated debate within the Prosecution of which you were a member of and in the final analysis or at the end of the day, to borrow your phrase, the decision was: Let's hold this and let's use it in the event the accused dares to exercise his right and testify on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. This talk of daring to use their right to exercise --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There are some problems, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that a major portion of the decision-making process, to withhold that information and then to be able to ambush the accused, in that case General Krstic, in the event he testified? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My part of the decision was with respect to whether or not it was going to be in my narrative and a part of my testimony. After I had made the decision that this is not something that I considered relevant, I am aware of the discussions that went on after that, and I believe, as I've testified, that the decision was made that this would be something that the Prosecution would hold and would attempt to use against General Krstic if he had testified and if he brought the issue up and made it relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: As a member of that team, given that you've now told us that in spite of it being authentic and reliable, you thought that it was not relevant at all in this case, did you forcefully argue during those debates that under no circumstances should they use this particular intercept which had the voice of none other than General Krstic, if we are to believe, you know, that is his voice? Did you argue against that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me cut your question into two parts on this one --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me the short version first. Yes or no, did you argue against it -- and then give your explanation, take your time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not argue against it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, give me your explanation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, with respect to importance of the case, there are two issues. My particular issue with importance to the case is whether it fell with respect to the Srebrenica crime scenes. Now, again, as part of the intercept authentication process, that is a very powerful piece of evidence, because in the event, as General Krstic indicated that he believed it was a forgery and certainly General Krstic or his Defence from the very beginning had indicated that they do not believe that the intercepts to be valid or reliable, whether this particular intercept fell inside or outside the actual scope of the commission of the crimes, it was a powerful piece of evidence that could be used to, in effect, corroborate some portion of the intercept collection process. Certainly, in that in mind, I was not prepared to argue against the use of that in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it not also corroborate somewhat the state of mind of the accused, that if he was willing to say such a thing to a young impressionable up-and-coming subordinate who graduated number one in his class and who was the deputy commander of one of the -- the largest brigade, in my understanding, of the Drina Corps? I mean, wouldn't that give us some inkling of his state of mind, and couldn't we then reason backwards and say, well, if this is how he's feeling post-Srebrenica, is it not reasonable to conclude, as we all might, that in all likelihood, he might be entertaining those sorts of thoughts, albeit we are unable to prove it beyond a reasonable doubt because we don't have some other smoking gun. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've highlighted the exact issue that I kind of hinge on from an analyst's perspective, is the fact that as a matter of practice taking material post event and then trying to extrapolate that back to the commission of the crime itself is not exactly a very sound practice. I mean, there's taking pieces of information that occur before and the ability to demonstrate that this is how it was then so you can draw that conclusion. But I don't think as a matter of analytical practice you can take something that happens well after the event and then try to string it back and say, see, this is how it related weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though it's related, because as you indicated, there were still Muslim men out in the woods in the vicinity of where the Zvornik Brigade was located trying to get themselves away from this madness, trying to save their lives. And here was a general telling his major, deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, kill them all. That's not some kind of -- there's no nexus, there's no connection, there's no linkage, there's nothing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the issue, if, in fact -- and see, "I have no way of knowing, those small pockets were armed men, whether they were trying to, quote, escape the madness or not, when combat was engaged in those areas, it is legitimate combat." Again, looking at the Zvornik Brigade reports for that period, there's no way I can conclude one way or another -- and in fact, some Zvornik Infantry Brigade reports, post-23 July 1995, there is an accounting of prisoners being taken, it makes it even harder for me to conclude that the orders being given on 2 August from General Krstic to Major Obrenovic are, in fact, to execute captured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is the analytical dilemma that I have in trying to get to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, going back to what you stated, one part of the debate, one aspect of the debate, dealt with withholding this information from the Defence so they would not have a long opportunity to come up with a well-rehearsed answer to what it was. Right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that, in fact, was part of the debate, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you fall on that part of the debate? Did you say, wait a second, we have article 20 and 21 of the statute, we have human rights, they're entitled to this information, the Rules of Evidence and Procedure allow us to give the -- for this disclosure, did you make that argument or were you with the camp of let's ambush them? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's now calling for a legal conclusion by referring to various articles that have not been brought up before. I'm objecting to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas --.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. We still have two questions to you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The first: Since this matter was mentioned in another case, we allowed you to move on with this line. But at the same time, I believe that you have to remember Rule 70, which is that the preparation of a case is not a subject to be disclosed. I hope you could not go into the very details of the discussions by the Prosecution in their office. Secondly, I believe that you have to establish some linkage between that case to our case, whether it's relevant to our case at this moment, because here we are only dealing with something which is closely relevant to your client and to your case. These are two remarks I would like to mention at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If I can go briefly and respond, Your Honour. Number one, there is an admission by the gentleman in his testimony that there was this debate and there was this strategy, so I'm not trying to pry into the sanctum sanctorum of the Prosecution, but it does seem to indicate that there was this strategy going on. Number two, it is relevant to our case because we have the same gentleman testifying here. And what I'm trying to demonstrate through this line of questioning that he's not some independent analyst that one would expect as an "expert" coming in, he's a member of the Prosecution team and as part of that member, on a very vital piece of evidence he took a strategic route in order to deprive the Defence of information that ultimately the Prosecution used on rebuttal. Thirdly, it's relevant because it never made it into his report. Now, the reason it never made it into his report is because by putting it in the report, they would have had to disclose it. But -- so that's how I think it's linked, because again if we go back to my questioning of the morning, it is not that I'm attacking anybody individually, but I am prosecuting the Prosecution for the manner in which they've investigated the case, and now as we see, the manner in which they're trying the case. I think it's good defence and at some point I will go into the specifics. But right now, I'm just hitting the general spots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, we are not debating this issue, but if you have any observations, you may raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karnavas has made these points. I think -- have any problem with these points. Judge Wald has very carefully dealt with the issue that the Judge was concerned about, and I think that the points have been made. I have no objection to those points and -- but we now seem to be getting involved in a repetition that is not going anywhere, frankly, and trying to repeat the same points over and over and over again. And that's my only comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you may move on, but bear in mind the objections from the Prosecution as well as the remarks from this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And try to make your cross-examination as concise as possible, because we already get the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I made those points, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask the gentleman in which camp he felt, the ones to disclose or the ones to hide, that's all. So I'll be more direct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which camp did you fall in during those discussions, the one to disclose or the one to hide? Just as -- so we can know for the record as the independent military analyst in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, if I recall correctly, once I was making the decision, I had made the decision that it wasn't relevant for me, I sat on the fence and watched what was a fascinating legal argument between the common-law people and the civil law people as to where it should place. And that is what I did with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Correct me if I'm wrong, just a follow-up question on this, if you're an independent military analyst and you're in charge of writing your report as objectively as possible and without any undue influence, would not the final call be yours to make -- to put it in, at least in the -- to err on the -- to err on a liberal side, in other words, put it out there with the caveat and let the parties at least be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Karnavas, once I made the decision not to use it, that it wasn't relevant, I expected that had I tried to include it for any reason, it would be perceived by all parties as me taking an unwarranted and unfair shot at the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But you didn't -- felt that once the Prosecution, your team, decided to use that in trial anyway?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was once the decision was made, they were going to use it in cross-examination, again, a fascinating legal argument developed around -- that they would be able to use it as a vehicle to impeach the testimony of General Krstic with respect to his truthfulness before the Court on having the conversation as well as to his analysis as to the reliability of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were -- and I said, fascinating discussions to be a party of and to listen to, but as someone who did not go to law school and is not versed in the differences between common law and legal law, that's where it's at. It was a fascinating discussion but nothing that I was a party to comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But of course you can understand others may take the other viewpoint that this was a means by which you particularly, and I'm speaking, Mr. Butler, you were trying to hide that information from the Defence and from the Trial Chamber. And I'm not saying this -- that you had some nefarious state of mind, but nonetheless the flip side to that could be that maybe you were trying to hide that evidence because that is what your handlers, if I can use that word, that is, the Prosecutors who were prosecuting the case, were instructing you to do. That could be a reasonable conclusion, too, could it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that an individual could make that a reasonable conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just very briefly, I know there's a science between military intelligence analysis, but if I could go with some of these concepts and tell me whether I'm in the right frame of mind and perhaps if we can get on the same wave channel we could get through the material for the rest of the week. I take it, it's the primary goal of military intelligence analysis to ultimately conclude or predict the probable actions or courses of actions that a foreign military or other collective body of persons on the battlefield would take under certain circumstances. This is military intelligence analysis, where things are ongoing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I mean, the whole focus of military intelligence analysis is, in fact, that it is designed to be predictive in nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And do not these conclusions require that the analyst maintain an objective, unbiased, and perhaps just as importantly, an open-minded approach in the course of that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, in fact, you could say that as a general principle for anybody who's analysing anything, if they intend to be an objective and an honest broker, so to speak, honest intelligence -- honest analyst. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you agree with me that you -- what you were producing for this particular Tribunal is not necessarily an intelligence analysis, but closer to what would be called perhaps in your parlance a historical military analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course that's vital because folks like you analyse a situation that has just occurred and, given those skills and tools you acquire through that process perhaps at a later point you may be faced in a situation where you may actually be doing military intelligence analysis, and you can draw from those experiences and tools that you have. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular instance, it's a seven-year period and it's just a continuing analysis of the events that occurred with respect to the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- sticking now with the historical military analysis. Are the techniques of military historical analysis similar to intelligence analysis, in that many of the analytical techniques are the same or similar, and the goal is to support a sound conclusion but this time of the completed actions of military units and/or of personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure in this perspective that works. I think you're kind of mixing the analytical metaphors between predictive analysis with respect to supporting a course or courses of action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And something which this, I consider is a much more broad contextual research. I'm not looking to specifically support any particular issue. I'm just kind of looking to lay out the context in as broad a complete framework as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Maybe I'm just not phrasing the question correctly, because I guess what I really want to say is: Does not your analysis, yours being in this historical military context that you're doing, require you to maintain an objective, unbiased, and open-minded approach in the course of arriving at your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If an unbiased analyst is attempting to document accurate, sound conclusions so that a consumer, such as us, for example a decision maker, trier of fact, can make an informed judgement. Is it wise or is it ethical to sort of slant or withhold -- to slant analysis or withhold potentially interesting, vital, relevant, authentic, and reliable information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no foundation for that. If he wants to talk to the Prosecution, Mr. Butler -- there has to be a foundation, a factual foundation for him to ask a question. He's asking it to the wrong people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And another thing, Mr. Karnavas, your question is too complicated. There are subjects to many, many interpretations from your question. Try to make your question as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to rephrase it slightly: If you're going to -- if one, not you in particular, but if an analyst is going to attempt to create an accurate and sound conclusion, in other words, he's going to act as an unbiased analyst, you would agree with me, would you not, that you would produce your work in a manner in which the decision maker would be in a position of actually discriminating what information they should give way to and what information they should not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, also as part of that analysis, you would want to make sure that in your presentation of your analysis, it is not slanted in one way or the other. In other words, there is no inherent bias, be it, you know, be it direct or indirect, intentional or unintentional?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, with respect to my own personal feelings and opinions, I try to keep them out as much as possible. However, with respect to bias, the one issue analytically speaking that remains out there is the fact that as -- myself personally as an analyst, and all analysts engaged in this field, we are limited to the amounts and types of information that we have available to us at the time. So if there is, in fact, a bias in one direction or another, it may very well be, in fact, because a lack of information. But as to your initial issue, I try as much as possible to keep any personal feelings or opinions out of the context of my report. And only when invited by either the Prosecution or you or the Trial Chamber will I make a subjective assessment as to a conclusion on that basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, let's switch to another topic. I want to talk a little bit about the intercepts in the general -- in a general sense and see if you would agree with me a little bit before we can actually get to the specifics. As I understand it, the intercepts were collected on or about 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- through 1998, there were a series of missions to my recollection where starting perhaps in December of 1997, first the -- what we call the spreadsheets or the dot matrix printout versions of the intercepts were collected, subsequently the notebooks, subsequently some of the audiotapes. And I believe through the course of 1999 and 2000, there were other missions which identified and collected either other notebooks or other intercept-related data. So it was, I believe, it was almost a two-year process in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, there was even what they call the intercept project?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that just for this particular case or is that sort of a project that exists for other cases? I don't want to go into specifics, but just merely to know the availability of resources in case you need to pull off some folks from one project, from one case, to put them on another because of expedited needs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this respect, the intercept project, I believe the investigation team for Srebrenica essentially put together the prototype project. It was a team and case-specific project with respect to the ABiH 2 Corps and MUP-related intercepts and notebook. So in that respect, the resources that they were able to put into that remained into it for almost all the duration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it Stephanie Frease was in charge of that project, and she, like you, was an integrated member of the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, by any chance, have some sort of role in determining the time frame as to when these intercepts would ultimately be translated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The intent of the team was that once we had designated July the 1995, the series of intercepts, first for organising and indexing and then ultimately for translation, we understood that we were trying to get them through as rapidly as possible, given the volume of the material in question.
