My issue with respect to time was that I had my report deadlines coming up, as was indicated by the Court, and my concern was I did not want to be in a position where I was reviewing intercepts or days of intercepts in isolation. As a matter of practice, what I wanted to be able to do was examine the entire block of intercepts over the time, you know, when I looked at it for the first time, so I would not get in a position where some things might jump out of context or things of that nature. So for me, that was my concern, that we would have the entire month done in the required time for me to analyse them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so -- and I understand you testified to this a little bit in the Krstic trial on your rebuttal. As far as I understand, you did not -- you were concerned not to fall into what you called an analysis trap by - and I think you just described that - by jumping to the conclusion with just some of the intercepts while not having the batch for the July intercepts all available for you to read, dissect, integrate, collate, in order to weave your fabric, which ultimately became the narrative. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In technical terms we call it analyse and synthesise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so, but correct me if I'm wrong, we're talking about one specific month, July 1995. And if we really want to be precise, as you noted, anything after the 23rd was not even relevant. So we're not even talking about the entire month of July, but more or less three weeks at best. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it -- well, let me ask you this: On the pecking order, on the order of hierarchy, were you above Ms. Frease, were you equals, were you parallel, were you on a different rug? How --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were equals and for the most part we were normally engaged in related but separate projects. Her background being more on the political side, and of course mine being on the military side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. She would focus on the intercepts and sometimes when need be, she would actually be in the field interviewing -- or assisting in the interviewing of those witnesses dealing with intercepts. And you on the other hand would also be in the field assisting at time, and we'll be getting to that, when certain military officials were being interviewed or other witnesses being interviewed that you deemed important enough to warrant your presence and assistance in the field. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, however, again, it wasn't ultimately my decision on when to go or when not to go. A lot of it were functions of budget and other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you were ordered. It wasn't like the military, like you got your order and you packed up and left whether you wanted or not to go to the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases I had more flexibility than being in the army, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I take it then that that was accomplished. In other words, you had the July intercepts transcribed and translated and available for you, all of them pertaining to Srebrenica, before and during your, was it, analysis and -- analysing and synthesising, that was the term you used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had all of that available?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not. Well, is there a particular explanation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In I believe it would be October or November of 2000 after my initial testimony, it is my understanding that the investigation team came across another approximately 20-ish notebooks, some of them which contained intercepts during that period, we integrated those into the process, and I believe certainly during the rebuttal case, I brought one or two of them up and I believe that the Defence brought several of them up as well. So in that context, because we did not physically have those in the office of the Prosecution, I did not include them in my contextual analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because it was too late?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after I had testified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Testified in direct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In direct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I take it on rebuttal you had the opportunity as we see on one occasion --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those issues were raised in the rebuttal case because they were considered to be something of relevance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand it from one of the corrections that you made on Friday, one particular intercept was helpful in you reaching a rather different conclusion than you had held previously with respect to one particular intercept which uses the phrase "up there." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that, but first I want to discuss this concept of this linguistic nuances of up there. As I understand it, Stephanie Frease was fluent in B/C/S. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She spoke it quite well, whether it was fluent or not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll we can get to her transcript. She did indicate she was quite well knowledgeable in the language. But she's not a native speaker, is she?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the background of where she learned the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She's not from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she's American.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She is a foreigner that has who learned another language?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But I take it behind her there were a group of people that were native B/C/S speakers, Bosnian, Serb -- Serbian and Croatian speakers. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I take it it was these folks that you were relying on in translating these intercepts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you received that translation, help me out here, was it your practice to perhaps sit down with a -- one of the -- I believe you guys called them language assistants, one of the language assistants to help you out in trying to figure out what -- any linguistic nuances that might be relevant in interpreting a particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear on the issue, translators and language assistants are two different classes of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, help us out there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that we work with are translators, they are the people who work with CLSS doing the final translations. Language assistants are individuals who have a working knowledge of the language but are not certified. That's why I just want to me you clear when we do these issues, these issues are discussed with the translators and ultimately with the revisers, not with language assistants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, well, thank you for correcting me. I actually didn't know that. And I hope I didn't sleight anybody. I take it from your answer you had the cream of the cream, because you said that you've got language assistants, you've got translators, and now you took the ones that did the polishing up assisting you when need be in interpreting any linguistic nuances that might be in intercepts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did the best we could and I had access to those, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, I'm rather curious. On this particular intercept, which has gotten so much attention at the Krstic trial and, of course, is getting some attention in this particular case, I would expect that this was an intercept that must have been highly analysed and debated back in the sanctum sanctorum of the Prosecution office right across the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. It appears we're going beyond Judge Wald's questions, which I thought were appropriate, into the analysis of the team regarding the specific intercepts. Mr. Butler's here to speak to his analysis. But the analysis of the team, I believe, is not appropriate on the Rule 70 grounds you had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we don't think that question is pertinent to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just one second. It took Mr. Manovic all of 30 seconds to figure out that up there does not mean north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, I'm wondering how it is, you know, whether this gentleman -- I want to ask him, did he ask his language assistants with respect to that particular phrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You could directly ask this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to lay some background into that to make sure I had a solid foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think I already know that's your point. You just ask this question to this witness to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recall asking a language -- or a translator, interpreter, to assist you in analysing this phrase "up there," if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe when we did the analysis of that particular phrase, the -- and I don't believe I discussed it specifically with a translator, my thought process was knowing that the general -- in the way that they talk with respect to up and down, my understanding, generally confirmed by my discussions with a number of the people that lived there, is that they will use the phrase up and down to describe the differences between the area known as upper Podrinje which is the area from Zepa and Gorazde and lower Prodinje which is the normal area from Vlasinica towards Zvornik. And that was -- generally when I look at the phrase up and down with respect to locations, that is one of the key things that I use. Now, the second piece with respect to up and down is, in fact, north and south. And in this particular context, I believe that the up there was in reference to north. It did not occur until I understood Mr. Obrenovic had discussed the issue that I had recognised that a third context from up and down could, in fact, be from the valley floor at the Drina River being down and the mountains in that area or the hills being referred to as up. In retrospect, this is a perfectly valid contextual analysis on that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I guess my question is, based on your answer, it would seem that at least, given that you didn't know the language -- I'm assuming that you're not fluent, but you did, in fact, recognise that there were two potential different interpretations. And then you came to learn later on that there was a third one. As an analyst, should you not have at least consulted and tried to figure out with one of the native speakers and see what they could, if it were possible, to guide you through this process so at least you could say, well, you know, I don't know exactly, they could be referring to this. They could be referring to that, instead of, this is what I think they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this respect, given the other intercepts that we had locating Colonel Popovic in Pilica at the time, I believe that it was a relatively straightforward analysis, and therefore I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But this particular intercept -- and we're going to dissect it. We're going to have to do some dissecting on this one too. This one, was it not critical in the Krstic case with respect to the massacre that took place in Branjevo Farm, at least with respect to one aspect of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was critical -- or I won't say critical, but it was important insomuch as one of the themes in the Krstic case was that General Krstic at the time had no knowledge of the commission of any of the crimes. And from that respect, a conversation occurring between Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and a member of the Drina Corps op centre discussing in part the commission of criminal acts was for me an important piece of inferential information, because as I conclude on a number of issues, if the Drina Corps op centre is aware of this issue, then it's -- logically assume that the commander should be as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I just want to touch on that a little bit. There is one aspect of this intercept which I think does not require such detailed analysis to come to a conclusion that Popovic, who's from the Drina Corps, was referring to certain events, which were criminal in nature. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if we look at that intercept, it becomes clear that there is another reference to up there, and that deals with the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what I'm trying to focus on. Because wasn't that a fact in the Krstic case -- and I'm not talking about what the Defence was trying to do. I'm talking about what the Prosecution and you were trying to establish, that through this particular piece of intercept, you could connect the Bratunac Brigade as follows: You have the testimony of Erdemovic, which he says men from Bratunac, and incidentally this is why I know there was no nefarious attempt on your part to mislead the Trial Chamber, but we had that, but you could never get Erdemovic to say brigade, and that was a question mark. And now all of a sudden you have this intercept and this intercept, if we give it the interpretation that you chose, would then lead us to believe that the men that came late, what we're referring to is when the man from the Bratunac came around 1.00 or 2.00 later in the midmorning, after the killings had already begun. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two pieces of information, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you weave those two pieces of information, and then you can begin at least -- and I'm not saying that that was the definitive piece of the puzzle, but it was one additional piece of confirmation in your mind which would assist you later to argue that those men that Erdemovic had talked about from Bratunac were, in fact, from the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From those two pieces, that those were the conclusions I drew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And part of that conclusion was based on your interpretation of the phrase "up there" in the contextual form that you gave it, even though you knew that there was at least one other possibility, and even though you did not speak the language, you never made a genuine -- well, maybe that's too strong a word, an effort to get some guidance as to whether up there could have a different meaning, thus giving the trier of fact an option to reach a different conclusion from the one that you had reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's indecipherable, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Butler is an extremely intelligent man and I know he's following me and he's reading the transcript as it comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the important thing is for us to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I truly apologise. Am I getting a cue that I was unintelligible at this point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer the question. In this respect, given my understanding of the context at the time, I certainly was willing to rule out that Colonel Popovic was somewhere in upper Podrinje, and again coupling that with other known facts that he was in Pilica during the day, I believe that the fair language meaning of that led me to the conclusion that when they said "up there," up there was Pilica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But again, the implication -- what I'm saying here is that you understood at that time -- you had enough sense of the language to know that there were two different interpretations. And my question is: As an analyst, would it not have been prudent to have at least entertained the other interpretation through the use of a highly qualified native speaker in order to get at least another opinion? Could that not have been prudent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be fair, Mr. Karnavas, I can't tell you that I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may very well have, I just don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess if you did, you could not be in -- you would not be a position today to explain to us how it is that Mr. Obrenovic was able to fill in the third option and your language assistant was incapable or not able to come up with a different interpretation that would have, that would have, at least with respect to one particular massacre, have been extremely exculpatory with respect to one individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is compound and clearly an argument. I don't see that as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is exculpatory, Your Honour. It's exculpatory to Colonel Blagojevic, because they didn't have that piece of the puzzle. It's only after Obrenovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would love to argue this case but these are arguments, these are not questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think it's almost time for a break. You might think over your question when we come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll make a break and we'll resume at 12.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I believe that during the break you have already been thinking of the rephrasing of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour -- well, I did do some thinking and I think that I've made my point on that issue. So I'm going to veer off to a slightly different course but continue in the same vein. And I want to apologise to the interpreters for speaking too fast. I understand we have been making it rather difficult for them and Mr. Butler and I will agree to speak a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, focusing your attention back to your testimony on Friday, I want to, again, go back to the question posed to you by the Prosecutor with respect to this additional intercept that you became aware of. The question was, and I'm reading from page 76, it starts with line 9, it says: "Now, do you have an intercept that you now incorporated into your analysis of this last part that you were not aware of at the Krstic trial?" And your answer was: "Yes." My question is: Was it that you were not aware of its existence because it had yet to be discovered at the time that you were preparing your report and testifying in Krstic, or were you not aware of it because it had not been translated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, that particular intercept was part of the, I believe, series of 27 or so books that were obtained in December, which would have been at the end of the Prosecution's direct case and moving on to the Defence case. I don't believe that I saw a translation of that particular intercept or series of -- basically it was a synopsis intercept during the rebuttal -- during the Defence case. And then professionally during the rebuttal case, I was already working on another case. So I was not following the Krstic material day-to-day. So certainly during the direct case and then during the cross-examination case, or the Krstic case, I don't recall seeing that particular document. I am aware that there was a translation available sometime during the rebuttal, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I take it you would be able to go back, you or the Prosecutor, would be able through the records and identify whether that was indeed one of the late batches that was discovered during the course of the investigation of this case. And I take it there is some means of keeping track when something is seized and --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe all that work has been done because that was an open issue in the Krstic appeal. I don't know whether you have access to that, but I know all that research was, in fact, done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, another question in the same mind, who is it charge of prioritising or, if I could use this term discriminating, which intercepts would get translated first and which, for instance, would get translated at a later date and which intercepts may never ever get translated, lest there be an interest on the part of the Defence, that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the initial batch of intercepts, the decision, partly as a recommendation from myself, Ms. Frease, and others who would be involved in the process and knowing the volume of work that had to be done, our recommendation to the trial team was that our priority of effort focus initially from 10 July 1995 to approximately 22 July 1995, which would correspond with the actual content of the crimes that are charged with respect to General Krstic at the time. There was then a secondary decision that once that was done from 23 July to the end of the month, and then as resources were available at the other end, from 1 July to 10 July. That is the recommendation that we made to the trial team, and I believe that it was accepted by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, did you give priority to, say, intercepts where there were actual conversations and perhaps less interest to synopsis or summaries of a conversation, or was it depending on content itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe the phrase was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All, okay. Well, I want to show you what has been marked as -- initially it was a Prosecution exhibit, P255/A and P255/D. We can put it on the ELMO. And actually, for the record, 255/A is the English version and 255/D is the typewritten version in B/C/S. If you could just look at that first. I would assume that you've seen this document, have you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does look familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could go to 255/D, and if we could put that on the ELMO, even though we don't read B/C/S, I think we might be able to glean something from this document. It seems, does it not, that portions are crossed off while one is boarded out so the text is -- stands out. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think if we went to the translated version and we looked at certain data, such as the time, the participants, even if we did not speak B/C/S, I think we could conclude, could we not, that these are the two -- the same documents, one in English, the other one in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fair conclusion. That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could share with you what was brought into this court before your testimony what has been marked for identification purposes as D75/1 and D76/1. Now, if you could just look at the pages first and you will note that there's a P255/F. And if you go to the second page of that, you'll see some handwritten text in B/C/S. If you look at that and then you can place it on the ELMO, if you would. Now, if you were to compare the English version with that handwritten text, at least with respect to the numbers, the hours and the names, it would appear, would it not, the name Blagojevic stands out as one of the names?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if you were to go to the -- if we were to go to 255/D, the one that we already looked at, and again compare the English version -- or D76/1, we see that now the handwritten version in B/C/S is typewritten, typed out, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, help me out here, if we look at -- and it becomes a little bit more legible, I think, if we look at -- if we compare the two documents of P255/D that you have, if you look at that, does it not appear that this particular synopsis comes immediately after the one that was blocked out and not crossed out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we were to read this document that has been translated, the one that was crossed out and not translated by the Office of the Prosecution, rather, it was translated by the Defence, if we were to look at it, do you see any information that would have been helpful to you in the contextual aspect of trying to determine Bratunac Brigade soldiers being sent towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this instance, would it be fair to conclude that someone - and I'm not suggesting it was you - but someone made a choice, the choice was to translate one portion and exclude another portion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could draw that inference, and I suspect that the answer why this particular conversation wasn't translated initially had something to do with the criteria by which we wanted material sorted and translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it wasn't translated --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that initially --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Full stop. It wasn't translated. We translated it. And if we look at the two intercepts side by side, one which appears to be a part of a conversation, while the other one seems to be a synopsis, although with some evidence or some information that you believe, based on your just testimony, to be relevant in nature, if we were to compare those two, can we not reach the conclusion that the one that was translated by the Office of the Prosecution is helpful to their case, while the other one, which is immediately below and which would be exculpatory in some sense or at least informative, particularly to a very relevant aspect of this case, was not translated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one interpretation. I'm not sure that it's the correct one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one was translated that was helpful to the Prosecution. And the one to the Defence was crossed out and not translated. So I guess what you're suggesting is you don't have an answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually I think I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please tell me why this information which I believe -- well, strike -- let me withdraw that. Please explain why this information which was translated by the Defence and which you find to be helpful, in particular to the other intercept, the one that we are in dispute over, the up there, and whether Bratunac Brigade soldiers participated in the Branjevo Farm massacre, why that piece of information, which is exculpatory in nature, which is immediately below the one the Prosecution translated, and which visibly has the name Blagojevic on it, why that wasn't translated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think with respect to the timing of the project, the initial decision on translating the intercepts, one of the decisions that we made in order to try and ensure that what we were doing was, in fact, translating authentic material, was the decision was made that the first translations would be and certainly any evidence that was going to be adduced before the Krstic Trial Chamber was -- had to have been from notebooks. As I believe I've testified prior, I don't -- with respect to just the printouts, the fact that a data is on a printout doesn't mean it's an authentic piece of material. With respect to your second question, while I can recall seeing this in a draft translated form, perhaps the reason why it's not included is that from my perspective, there is a better intercept that's more complete, which is the notebook version of what we call P258 which is the actual synopsis of the conversation which indicates when Colonel Blagojevic's troops arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Are you telling me today, because I need to know this, that this piece of information was actually translated by the OTP and it wasn't discovered and disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall seeing this piece of information in some of our working drafts. I suspect that if this material is out there, it has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if I were to tell you that I had to have it translated because it wasn't translated by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wouldn't surprise you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, now you said -- you mentioned the word authentic, and that piqued my interest immediately. Because you said one of the indicia it would have to come from a notebook?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the initial stages, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the initial stages. Well, it just so happened I anticipated that response because here I provided you both the handwritten version which matches, low and behold, the typewritten version in B/C/S. So can we conclude, at least with this particular intercept, which came from a notebook, which was in the possession of the Prosecution, is indeed authentic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would conclude that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I understand your position and I understand that you were not the one making all of these decisions, because obviously you don't read the language and you are handicapped in relying on others to follow your instructions or the decisions. However, in looking at this, just gleaning just at this piece of information that we just discussed, does it not appear, at least, that in some ways, some evidence that would have been helpful to you was actually available to you; it simply wasn't made available to you because somebody in your own team chose not to have it translated for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That assumes a fact and not an evidence, that somebody specifically chose this not to translate. We clearly didn't translate everything, but if he's going to make accusations like that he has to have foundation. The implication is obvious. He's trying to pick on our interpreter, which is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me clarify it. Let me clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From looking at this document, it's obvious one follows the other. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From looking at this document, one was highlighted and the other one was crossed out. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would assume that one would not cross intercepts without at least reading them to see whether they're relevant to the issue at hand. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, just to be accurate on this document, I don't have cross-out versions of this. The cross-outs that exist on these versions, as I understand the translation process, are only with respect to the process themselves. So when the draft translations are sent for final revision, that the translators know exactly which one to focus on and aren't doing the wrong job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So these cross-outs are not for my benefit or exclusion, they are a strict translation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify that, for the same reason so the exhibits can be made clear which ones are relevant at the time, the bottom and the top were crossed out so it was clear which of the B/C/S exhibits the Court could focus on. That's what's going on here. This is not some nefarious crossing out going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe that's the suspicions that the Defence counsel had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In looking at this document, the way it was presented to us from the Prosecution in the crossed-out form, would it not leave one with an impression that someone chose to focus on one and disregard the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to relevance, Your Honour. That is an argument he may make. The Court asked, but there is no relevance for Mr. Butler to make that unfounded speculation at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Butler has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was one new piece of information, this new intercept, that was able to assist you in overcoming a fixed position that you had initially reached during your analysis, and I'm paraphrasing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be accurate, I'm an analyst. I don't have fixed positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am always, as a function of my trade, as new data or new information comes in, I put it where it belongs in context. So I don't have fixed positions on anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, the follow-up question where -- that we were -- going back to your testimony on Friday, you were asked, page 76, now I'm reading from line 13: "But before we get to it, can you tell me initially, what was the issue related to the arrival of Blagojevic's men?" That was the question. Here is your answer: "That view initially migrated over several years with respect to my analysis of the situation. Based on Erdemovic's statement and testimony at his own trial as well as the documents that we received from the Bratunac Brigade, my initial conclusion" - and I underscore initial - "my initial conclusion was that these people were probably from the Bratunac Brigade. As a following series of that investigation continued, the investigation was able to identify an individual who was known to be a member of the Panteri unit from the East Bosnia Corps and who were in Bratunac in July 1995. And I believe that has been brought to this Court's attention. When that part of the information became available and I was able to analyse it and synthesise it in the context of the Krstic trial, I testified to that effect during the rebuttal case of the Prosecution where I noted that my position on that had changed based on new information." Now, do you recall making that -- giving us that answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if we take it from the top, you had an initial point of view that you formed as a result of the Erdemovic statement and other documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a theory. It wasn't a point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say -- you were asked about your views and you say: "That view initially migrated," it left, you know, it was moving. "Over several years with respect to my analysis of that situation." And then you say: "Based on Erdemovic's statement and testimony at his own trial," and let me stop there. During that process, he never ever, according to you and based on the evidence that we have, said that it was men from the Bratunac Brigade. Okay. So, based on that information as well as the documents that we received from the Bratunac Brigade, my initial, my initial, conclusion was that these people probably were -- were probably from the Bratunac Brigade. Now, at what point in time, sir, did you migrate all the way to the other end and determine that those people were not indeed from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the full migration on that would have been -- what month are we in now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're in November.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it would have been about March or April of this year when the OTP acquired from the Zvornik medical centre a notation from the individual - I won't mention his name - that indicated that he was treated at the Zvornik Infantry Brigade -- or at the Zvornik medical centre on 15 July 1995. So for me, that is the conclusive piece of evidence, that particular piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so during the Krstic trial you still maintained --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just for the record. I think there was a mistake on the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The date --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry 16 July 1995. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That date. Thank you. We need to slow down, too. We're both getting a little excited here. Now, I take it during the Krstic trial and throughout that trial, you still maintained your position at that point in time, given the information that had been made available to you and based on your analysis and synthesis of that information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several stages. During the direct part of the Krstic trial, that was my initial one. We started developing information on this individual. And during the rebuttal phase, I brought that information forward. Primarily they used me as a vehicle to provide information which was believed to be Rule 68 on that regard. We continued the investigation on that, and in respect for me -- as I said, the key conclusive piece was to find a piece of documentary evidence that had that specific individual in that area on 16 July 1995. So in synopsis, that represents about a two and a half year's worth of migration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say we're finally home, that you finally have determined that when Erdemovic says men from Bratunac, they were not from the Bratunac Brigade? Are we there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's never say never on this issue. We're good on one identification. There may be a potential identification for another. I'm willing to conclude at this point that they were not men assigned to the Bratunac Brigade, and I believe I've said that. And I certainly don't indicate that in my report, that they were from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But until we get the full identities, I'd prefer to leave it an open issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And of course another piece of the puzzle that is assisting you in addition to this medical record is the fact that we now have a clear interpretation as to that other intercept that was relied on to some extent, I would like to say heavily, but there may be some equivocation on whether it's heavily or significantly or to some extent, in determining that when they said "up there," it meant that Blagojevic's men from the Bratunac Brigade arriving at the Branjevo Farm up there later for the executions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, while that is one interpretation, for me the more and to use the phrase exculpatory issue on that is not where up there is, but for me it's the intercept that indicates that the forces from the Bratunac Brigade did not arrive until well after the executions could have been finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to get to that. We're going to get to that. Now just -- and before we get to it, I just have a minor question. Did you by any chance write up a revised or an updated version to your revised version or provide something in writing of this new migrated position that you now hold, because as you've indicated, that was several months ago. And here we are in November in trial, and certainly I might have been a little more efficient in my time and preparation in cross-examination also had I had something from you. Did you do something in writing and present it to the Prosecution for them to disclose to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue was discussed with the Office of the Prosecutor, and my understanding is it was felt that the best vehicle to do this was actually through the individual himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was that a decision that they made or you as the independent analyst, or was it something that you both sort of sat around and decided on a coordinated basis to just wait until trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas had this material well before trial and that's a misstatement of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's incorrect, Your Honour. I was unaware of his total migration. This is quite new to me that he's migrated all the way to the other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the migration issue is just mentioned during this trial. But, Mr. Karnavas, you have already had that intercept already; that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Without translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour, and it was my intention to prove Mr. Butler wrong. Thankfully, and I didn't know this at the time, but thankfully he came in and explained it and took the wind out of my sails. But at least it was an admission, we're grateful for it, but nonetheless had we known in advance, we could have been a little bit -- we could have channelled our energies in a different direction. And I think this is a fair statement to make, especially when we have limited resources. But I'm going to move on, Your Honour, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving on but we're still sort of on the migration topic, but in a different direction. I want to go through with you if we could some of the documents that you had available to you at the time to see whether, through those documents, you might have been just as equally able to reach another plausible and alternative explanation, if you will. So with that, if we could go down the road to these documents, I would like now to go through what has been marked as P490 for identification purposes. I'm going to go through a series -- actually I'm going to hand -- I would like you to have P490, P534, P496, P531. I think you already have handy and you might want to keep them over there, D76/1, P258. This is the one that, as I understand, the new one that you received, but just for contextual purposes I think we should keep it into the mix for the discussion. P534 and P540. And if you could get the documents assembled, then we'll go through them in a sort of chronological order and see whether these documents, with the exclusion, excluding the one that you had, but with the information from other documents would have told you a story that might have been as equally plausible to the one that you had determined prior to your migration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're going to need a break. That's going to take Mr. Butler some time to pick out all those various exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe they were introduced, weren't they.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course introduced. But there are so many documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm not suggesting that -- we can go through one by one. It might be easier that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, find the most convenient way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have 490 up and on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, my apologies to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for clarify, Mr. Butler has his own collection of these exhibits for simplicity, and so he's taking his -- from his own collection, just so it's clear. They should be identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document was generated on 15 July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe if we look at the bottom, you've indicated that it was sent at 1725, which would have been 5.25 in the afternoon on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at -- if we could focus on paragraph 2 and we focus at the second sentence where it says: "Part of our forces have been sent to the area of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, 80 soldiers, and an S-2M platoon has been sent in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade area of responsibility." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was this information available to you as part of the documents during the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would suspect that you received this document when you searched the Bratunac Brigade headquarters? I don't know. I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would have been, what, 1998? 1997?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been early 1998, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, clearly this tells us a little bit, right, this little piece of information, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We do know one thing, that on this particular in the Zvornik area, there was heavy fighting going on where the Zvornik Brigade took in a lot of casualties and there was, in fact, quite a bit of concern that Zvornik would fall. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so -- and over here from this information, we see that 80 soldiers are being sent from the Bratunac Brigade to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the second document, and that would be P534. If it will be easier, I have mine handy. I'm used to approaching the witness, but ... Now, if we look at this document, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date is 15, 16 July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14, 15 July on this page, sir. Is this the one you want up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have -- I believe this was 5 -- page 7, I'm sorry. Page 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a part of the collection of the duty officer reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the Zvornik garrison logbook, not the duty officer logbook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was this, by the way, available to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the documents that Obrenovic provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we can assume that you didn't have this piece of information when you were -- until recently. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in this document, we see that the period of time it's covering is between 15 and 16 July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we see -- if we go to the second bullet, it says about 1000 hours, a new shift of the Bratunac Brigade arrived which was sent to the field some time later. And I take it that would have been 10.00 in the morning on the 15th, since this is a 24-hour period daily reporting system. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at P496/A, and again I have it here available for you. This is a daily combat report, is it not, dated 16 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is from the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it you had -- this document you did have for your analysis and synthesis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look in paragraph 2, sort of in the middle of it, there's a section -- there's a sentence which begins with: "We made preparations to dispatch two companies to the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade (100 soldiers) and the 4th Reconnaissance Platoon of the 1st Infantry Battalion." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we go all the way down, we see that this was signed at 1640, that would be 4.40 p.m., which was right about the time when the daily combat reports were usually due and sent out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this piece of information which you had available obviously sort of supports what's happening on the ground as well, and that is that the Zvornik Brigade needs help, you had information that they were asking for help, particularly from the Bratunac Brigade, and here it is -- we have a daily combat report that more or less validates all of that information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn to P531. And again I have my copy. They're marked at the bottom. If you could look at this. You recognise this document, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this document available to you at the time you were doing your analysis and synthesis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as we could see, this was generated from the Zvornik Brigade. It's an interim combat report, and it's dated 16 July 1995. Is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we were to go down to paragraph 2, it says: "Our forces (Zvornik, a company of the MUP Ministry of the Interior of 100 men, two platoons from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and the part of the military police platoon from the IBK Eastern Bosnia Corps) are carrying out a decisive defence in the brigade zone, sealing off and searching the terrain in the wider area," and then it goes on. Decisive defence, you have heard that term before, have you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact that is exactly what was happening on the ground, there was a decisive defence, given that the Zvornik Brigade was all of a sudden facing two fronts, the column and of course the 2nd Corps that was also attacking from another direction in order to assist the column to pass through. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from this piece of information, the interim combat report available to you, which also states here it was sent out at 1610 hours, that's on July 16th. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe 1810 hours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1810 hours. Okay. And that would have been 6.10 p.m. On that particular day. This piece of information also validates not only what is happening on the ground but also the fact that the Bratunac Brigade had been asked to assist and send some troops to the Zvornik Brigade for the purposes of engaging the column and the 2nd Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just so we're clear, that was a purely military operation very consistent with the laws of war, if I could put it in the general context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military operation. I will reserve judgement on how consistent it was, only insomuch as we have no data one way or the other with respect to any wounded or prisoners from the column. So I'll just reserve judgement on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as the actual asking assistance and providing assistance to the Zvornik Brigade during that critical moment, that in and of -- that act, that was not an illegal act, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Those are all proper and diligent exercises of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. See, we can agree on some points. Now, if we can go to -- the next one is the P255/D, we've already looked at it, but nonetheless let's look at it again. If I may -- you can have -- 255/D, we just covered it, but again, you know -- forgive me, I'm not sure whether I asked you this question, but was this available to you when you did your analysis and synthesis? And I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document in question, this particular one or this one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one that I translated --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular one, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly what time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry this was --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- It became available to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. This is a document you generated and this is the new information. So for the record, this is the one --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document, 258 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, 255/D is the one that I am told -- let me give you another document, and I apologise again for the confusion here. But if we give you -- if we can give you 258 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 258.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Now 258 is this new document which you as -- you have indicated was very helpful in the migration process. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course we have presented to you what is marked as D76/1, which is immediately below, and you would agree with me, would you not, that this also -- this was the one that was below the one that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I take it this would also -- well, on this particular one, can you tell us whether you had this one available to you, in other words, whether it was in the possession of OTP, not whether it was translated or not, but whether it was in their storage at the time that you were doing your analysis and synthesis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not exactly tell you at what point in time it came into the possession of the OTP. We can obviously get that answer. I can say that at a point in time I do remember seeing this because just the series of three bullets on Colonel Cerovic as the duty officer calling places. So that's why to me this looks very familiar, but I couldn't tell you specifically at what point in time I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you would agree with me, this one is generated on the 16th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at the hour, it's 2006, that's 8.06 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would appear that again here is yet another piece of information that validates the fact that the Bratunac Brigade has sent men to a designated place where there's an ongoing battle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The only thing that we're unclear of at this point in time is whether you had it, whether it was in the OTP's possession at the time you were doing your analysis and synthesis. But let me ask you this: Had you come across this, would you have deemed this relevant and important in factoring your decision on whether the Bratunac Brigade men were sent to Zvornik to assist in a battle versus the Erdemovic conundrum, if I can call it that, of whether those men were members of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, given insomuch as it is a call for reinforcements, it would be a part of that relevant mix. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can go to the next document, which is P534 -- I'm sorry. I think we've already covered that. But if that -- well, I'm sorry. You have the document P534, if we could go to page 8.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just refresh my memory on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the second document that we covered the duty operations report from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You got it back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can't find it -- here, take my copy. I'll wing it. If you could look at that. If you could put it on the ELMO, maybe I can follow it. This is page 8, is it not, it's even underlined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's page 8 of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this one covers the period of the 16th to 17th, that 24-hour period. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, as I understand it, that period begins around 8.00 in the morning. So it would be 8.00 to 8.00?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am less familiar with the actual garrison duty officer functions as to when that started and stopped. But I think that's fair. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I marked an area -- one line which says: "Forty men who were not members of the Zvornik Brigade stayed overnight." Now, I believe you indicated earlier that -- and I believe it was on direct examination this morning where you indicated that some members of the Bratunac Brigade had gone astray and had to stay overnight. Was this this group or was this another group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember the context of that correctly, that particular group was essentially the first two platoons of the Bratunac Brigade that arrived on the 15th from the 4th Company. They were deployed into the field, and during the context of the combat that evening, they were separated from the main defensive positions, spent the night moving through the woods. They came out on the main road sometime in the late morning hours of 16 July, and from there they went to the school at Orahovac. So I don't recall whether from the school at Orahovac, whether they went back into the field. I believe the commander of that detachment indicates that in his interview with the OTP, that after that series of events occurred, that they immediately then returned to the Bratunac Brigade area. So I don't know that I could conclude that it's in fact those people who are staying overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any witnesses giving any statements to the effect that some members of the Bratunac Brigade had stayed at the headquarters of the -- or had stayed at the Zvornik Brigade on that particular night? I mean, if you know, fine, if not ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they were staying at the headquarters of the brigade. I think there were some elements out in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be with respect to the second group that had arrived, but -- okay. If you don't recall, you don't recall. Now, let's -- and this piece of evidence was also available to you, although as we've noted, it's not very conclusive at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This particular piece of evidence came with Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one here. Okay. Now, the last document would be 540, P540. And you have already commented on this. Now, once again this is the interim combat report, and it's dated 18 July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, it appears to have the name of the commander, Pandurevic, himself. Now, if we could look at the second paragraph. The second paragraph indicates: "The Zvornik Infantry Brigade forces, reinforced by a company from the Krajina 16th Brigade, a company from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, two platoons of the Bijeljina military police, and one platoon from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade successfully repulsed all enemy attacks from the front, sealed off and searched the terrain in the wider area of Crni Vrh, Pandurica, Krizevici as well as completely securing the old and the new Zvornik Crni Vrh roads." So it would appear from this report that we have some validation that there is a company there from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we've gone through these documents, I guess my question is this: It would appear that you had, albeit not all of these documents, several documents which were consistent with what was happening on the ground, and that is documents demonstrating that members from the Bratunac Brigade had been sent to Zvornik for military purposes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I guess my question is: If we were to take these documents that were available to you at the time, analyse them, and synthesise them, and then go on to look at that intercept, the one of July 16th, would that -- armed with that information and knowledge and knowing what was happening at the time, should it not have given you some pause that perhaps there was another interpretation to the phrase "up there"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I've certainly never disputed the fact that the bulk of the forces were engaged in combat operations. However, given the fact that one of the two correspondents in the exhibit that we're discussing is the assistant commander for security of the Drina Corps, that was for me a significant piece of information. And having his prior knowledge established in Pilica, that is how I concluded that within the context of that intercept, that's where up there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But correct me if I'm wrong, on Friday you had given us a little peek into the process by which you discriminate information and how you reach an analysis. And as I understand it -- well, let's, just to be a little more precise, let's look at page 71 of the transcript. And I'll just read it -- I have it here for the ELMO. It's a short piece. It would be instructive, I believe. And of course I'm not repeating anything you haven't already said. But -- now, I'm going to be focusing on lines 1 all the way to line 8. So you're asked a question by the Prosecutor. "Q: So why are you changing your mind?" And your officer is, this past Friday, November 14th, you state: "In this context, and I always try to note as a component of my total analysis, if a document or an intercept was open to multiple interpretations, particularly in the issue between a criminal interpretation and a strictly military one, that as a matter of practice when it was I would always default back to that military interpretation. That's how I professionally view it, a component of attempting to keep my analysis of the material as conservative as possible." Now, do you recall giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so if I understand what you're trying to tell us here is that when in doubt, when in doubt, where there's -- it's subject to various interpretations, you're going to err on the side of caution. And -- in other words, if it's between military and criminal, you would err on the side of criminal and therefore -- on the side of the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As much as I could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because after all, you want to be fair. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I want to or not, the process makes me be fair, and that's what I try to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is why I'm asking you this question. With this particular intercept, you've already indicated to us that you were aware that up there had two different linguistic meanings. And now we also see that you had some documentation, albeit not all of it, but some, which would -- and you also had all of this other knowledge as to what was happening on the ground. And so when I analyse it and when I synthesise it, it would appear to me that another interpretation is equally available to you, particularly if you want to err on the side of caution. Would you not agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that, as I've discussed, at the time I made my initial analysis of that, that my interpretations of the linguistics were with respect to up there being Pilica and up there being upper Podrinje. So I think I've covered that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You covered that issue. But you see, I'm putting it in the, as you put it, the historical context. See I'm doing a little synthesising myself here and I'm asking you to help me out, because you certainly had all this information. You knew what was happening on the ground. You had some intercepts and other documents that coincided with what was happening on the ground. And then there was this intercept where there might have been a dilemma by what was meant by up there. So my question is: If you could please give us your analysis, the analytical process by which you decided to discriminate that information that was available to you. And in doing that, I would also like you to include in your answer as to why perhaps you never included into your analysis the possibility that up there could mean something else, as you knew it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. Again, this is a nice argument, but it's indecipherable from the -- and if that kind of question is going to continue, we'll never get finished. This doesn't make any sense and it's the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. McCloskey. But since we have little time available for the morning session, we'll hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have what you were asking. If -- again, for me where it becomes very clear on the multiple meanings, and again as I've noted before, it's -- for me the issue of where up there was was less relevant than when the reinforcements arrived with that respect. Now, again looking at the issue of up there, I would go back to what I had said previously on that, which is that given the prior intercepts and information of Popovic being at Pilica. Now, again in fairness to Mr. Karnavas here, perhaps the one real interesting piece of information that I didn't have at the time that I wish I had, are the reflections on the Obrenovic duty officer logbook for 16 July, which specifically reflect that the Drina Corps is instructing Colonel Popovic to stop what he's doing and immediately track down Colonel Pandurevic at the time and get an explanation as to what is going on. So like I said, looking at the totality of the information, that's why it's very easy for me at this point to conclude what Obrenovic said about it is, in fact, probably the most accurate conclusion that could be drawn, that up there is in fact the IKM area at Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last follow-up question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there not multiple interpretations available to you, based on all the information that you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are multiple interpretations, but I didn't believe that that one was a reasonable one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you didn't put in your report and to your analysis the other ones and try to reason them out and demonstrate as to why those were less plausible, less believable, less possible than the one that you zeroed in on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the context of my report, I try to support the conclusions that I make. It would be a very long report if I had to go through each and every alternative possible conclusion and, you know buttress that up as well. I believe I did an adequate job -- I believe I did certainly a fair job in explaining my conclusion at the time. And I believe I have been able to indicate what is the basis of new information that has caused me to change that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my question and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He did --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsels not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I believe the witness has already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you look at his response, he says he apologises, acknowledging that he didn't. He gave an explanation. It was a very direct question. Now, maybe from that answer we can draw an inference, but I would like to get a clear answer, whether he gave us the other possibilities and then excluded them. And it's a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could leave this question until tomorrow. Now it's time for the break. And I have to remind the parties tomorrow we'll sit in courtroom I in the afternoon from 2.15 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one other minor request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a request made by the Prosecutor last week so that Mr. Butler could consult with the members of the -- other members of the Prosecution, particularly those involved in the Krstic 115 matters and the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point in time given the critical juncture we are and given that he had plenty of time, or they have had plenty of time to have access to Mr. Butler, I would ask that from this moment on that they have no contact whatsoever with Mr. Butler regarding this case or the Krstic case. And if it becomes that necessary, that I certainly would like to be present in addition to somebody from the registry, because I think that I'm pretty familiar with the case. But I don't want in any way any discussions about this case and I'm not suggesting anything, it's just this has always been my practice and I would feel much more comfortable if we could abide by that rule, because they -- there is no real reason for them to need Mr. Butler, since they have -- he's been here for several weeks and I'm sure they've had plenty of time to iron out all of their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Karnavas is right on that point, and I don't see a problem with that. Mr. Butler may be happy not to talk about this anymore. But if I could -- let me just -- before we tie the appeal's hands and the Appellate Chamber on these issues. If I could just check, and I think that's the case, and I hope it's the case, but if I could just check with the appeals people on that. I have no objection with Mr. Butler not dealing with them at all until I can check. And if there is some issue, then maybe we can talk about it tomorrow, but I hope there isn't, like Mr. Karnavas. But let me check with them first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that is a reasonable request. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
